newsitem.title: NORWAY: Flood gates open under Icelandic glacier.
newsitem.headline: Flood gates open under Icelandic glacier.

text.p: A giant lake under Europe's largest glacier in southeastern Iceland began flooding on Tuesday in a delayed reaction to a volcanic eruption beneath the ice cap last month, a scientist said.
"The flood started in the Skeidara river about three hours ago," Magnus Tumi Gudmundsson, a geophysicist at the University of Iceland in Reykjavik, told Reuters by telephone.
"The water has started to seep out from many parts (of the glacier) and it's rising very fast," Gundmundsson said.

Iceland has been preparing for flooding of the uninhabited black sand plains at the foot of the Vatnajokul glacier since a volcanic eruption melted parts of the ice cap and filled the sub-glacial lake Grimsvotn to overflowing.
A reporter with Icelandic National Radio said the flood waters had descended faster than forecast.
"In three hours 6,000 cubic metres of water has come down. People can already see iceblocks on the plains and they expect the bridges to disappear in a few hours," he said.

Emergency services said workers measuring water levels of the many rivers and tributaries crossing the plains had been forced to pull out of the area because of the speed of the torrent, which scientists had previously estimated could surge out at up to 25 metres (80 feet) per second.
"The water is running extremely fast down onto the sands. There's not so much we can do. We can just watch and wait," said a spokesman for the emergency services in the Icelandic capital Reykjavik.

The eruption subsided in mid-October but the North Atlantic island has remained on alert for the expected floods, which could destroy the country's one coastal ring road and bridges and power and telecommunication lines passing through the area.
Authorities have been preparing for the torrent by reinforcing dykes and building channels to steer the flood of water, debris and iceblocks away from infrastructure.
The Vatnajokul glacier stretches over 8,300 square kilometres (3,200 sq miles) and reaches in parts a depth of 1,000 metres (3,000 feet).
